newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania offers new pyramid refunds amid confusion.
newsitem.headline: Albania offers new pyramid refunds amid confusion.

text.p: More of the hundreds of thousands of Albanian investors duped by pyramid investment schemes were to collect partial refunds on Wednesday, but the launch of the payouts was marked by confusion and frustration.
Authorities appeared prepared to take whatever measures necessary to guard against anger among savers boiling over into fresh unrest in Europe's poorest country.
Refund schemes have been announced for only two of five failed investment funds six years after the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime.
But only a handful of 150,000 investors due to receive 60 percent of their deposits from seized funds of the Populli scheme collected hard cash at designated curbside booths.
More than 200,000 people were to begin claiming back even less -- 52 percent -- from the Xhaferri programme on Wednesday. Half the potential claimants were in the capital.
"You are all thieves," muttered a frail man who turned up at a payout point with faded yellow receipts to find himself left off an official list. He was told to come back in a week.
Bank officials said virtually all claimants demanded cash, refusing the alternative of government certificates. Some refused partial payout and demanded their entire stake.

Right-wing President Sali Berisha, speaking after round table talks on Tuesday boycotted by most opposition parties, offered help to worst-hit depositors, particularly those who sold homes to pump money into the schemes.
But he said the government could not fuel inflation by promising more than it was able to provide.

Government fears of new trouble focused on southern Albania, where furious depositors set fire to government buildings last month, after the head of a third scheme in the port city of Vlore told national television he was broke.
"It is true I promised depositors their money back, but I have none to give," Fitim Gerxhalliu said. "I ask investors not to come to reclaim their money. I am trying to cash in assets."
Police set up roadblocks on the main road leading to Vlore and refused entry to motorists with out-of-town registrations.
Television news broadcast for the fourth consecutive day appeals from prominent and ordinary Albanians to refrain from violence -- this time from two southern towns.
Tirana's foreign community appeared wary. The U.S. embassy preschool closed for two days as payouts got under way.
But the arrest of about 150 demonstrators on public order charges and pledges to mete out long prison sentences kept protesters away from new rallies last weekend.
Television said prosecutors had speeded up proceedings against alleged violators.
Berisha, whose Democratic Party retained power last May in elections denounced by observers as fraudulent, rejects charges that his government failed to warn investors.
Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million put money into the pyramid programmes, under which interest to older investors is paid out with deposits from new customers.

Opposition parties have called for the government's resignation. They were joined in their demand by exiled king Leka Zogu, who told a Tirana monarchist daily from South Africa that Berisha's administration was corrupt beyond redemption.
